title: Guest editorial: AI and ethical consumerism among young consumers
abstract: In a world increasingly shaped by intelligent algorithms, the relationship between young consumers and artificial intelligence (AI) warrants critical scholarly attention. AI is no longer a distant innovation. It is embedded in the digital platforms, applications and experiences that shape the everyday decisions of young people. From algorithmic product recommendations to AI-driven sustainability scoring and agentic AI, these technologies increasingly mediate not just what young consumers buy, but how they think, act and relate to broader societal and environmental issues.This special issue of Young Consumers on Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Consumerism among Young Consumers emerged from a growing recognition that current discussions around AI and youth consumption often overlook a fundamental dimension – ethical consumerism. As highlighted by Berki-Kiss and Menrad (2022), while technological advancements have enabled convenience, personalization and efficiency in consumer decision-making, they bring to the fore new concerns about ethical responsibility, transparency, inclusion and moral agency. These concerns are especially pronounced among younger consumers, who are simultaneously tech-savvy digital natives and often recognized as value-driven ethical agents.At its core, ethical consumerism is about aligning one’s consumption practices with personal and collective moral values (Kim et al., 2022). It encompasses concerns about responsible leadership (Tan, 2023), environmental sustainability (Eijdenberg et al., 2025; Gabler et al., 2022), fair labor practices (Berki-Kiss and Menrad, 2022) and corporate transparency (Lii and Lee, 2011). Research such as Abulibdeh et al. (2024) has shown that young consumers prioritize these issues, demanding authenticity, accountability and equity from the brands they support. In other words, young consumers can be catalysts for positive consumption change.Yet, the growing popularity of AI agents and their different capabilities results in layers of complexity and consequences upon their interactions with users (Noor, 2024). For instance, AI-enabled recommender systems are designed to make suggestions by prioritizing user purchasing patterns. While this is convenient, such systems can obscure critical information and reinforce existing biases (Gomez-Uribe and Hunt, 2015). Similarly, AI-enabled chatbots and virtual influencers may project desirable images that subtly promote materialism or reinforce stereotypes. These trends demonstrate that the responsibilities for information filtering, judgment and decision-making are increasingly delegated to machines. Naturally, questions arise about the diminishing ethical agency of consumers. Are young people being empowered or disempowered by AI in their consumption choices? Are their values being reflected or manipulated by the technologies they engage with daily?With this special issue, our goal was to bring together scholars who could integrate these complex and often paradoxical relationships between AI and ethical consumerism in young people. We sought to move beyond the hype and techno-optimism in the marketing and AI literature, and instead probe deeper into how AI technologies influence, enable, constrain or even redefine ethical behavior among youth.Several key themes emerge from the rich articles featured in this special issue. These span important and diverse issues in the AI–young consumer ecosystem, ranging from sustainable behaviors and identity, to engaging young consumers effectively and ethically, and ultimately continuing to create safe use environments with evolving AI technologies such as Generative AI.Encouraging sustainable consumption behaviors remains a key theme, with several studies supporting AI’s potential to foster environmentally and socially responsible consumption. For instance, the qualitative study “AI’s Influence on Young Consumer Behavior: Fostering Sustainable Consumption” by Lata and Rana (2025) and the quantitative studies “Influence of Artificial Intelligence on Consumers’ Lifestyle Product Choices and the Key to Driving Sustainable Behaviour” by Mahajan et al. (2025) and “Assessing the Influence of Artificial Intelligence on Sustainable Consumption Behavior and Lifestyle Choices” by Sharma and Sharma (2025) investigate how AI can guide young consumers toward more conscious, sustainable lifestyles. These studies suggest that AI, when designed with ethical and environmental considerations, can play a pivotal role in empowering youth to align their consumption with their values.Beyond consumption patterns, AI also shapes how young consumers engage with their identities and cultural preferences. Thomas et al.’s (2025) comprehensive mixed-methods study “From Beats to Bytes: Electronic Dance Music, Artificial Intelligence and Teens Identity” offers a novel exploration of how AI intersects with youth culture, particularly in the formation of identity and community through music. This work expands the conversation from ethical buying behavior to the broader sociocultural impacts of algorithmic mediation in youth experiences.Another area of inquiry by Marti-Ochoa et al. (2025) focuses on how AI-generated personas and influencers affect young consumers’ ethical choices. Specifically, their sentiment-analysis study “AI-Driven Virtual Travel Influencers and Ethical Consumerism: Analysing Engagement with Sena Zaro’s Instagram Content” identifies the adherence to ethical communication standards and evaluates the types of content that garner the highest engagement. This study differentiates from many similar other studies by challenging us to reconsider authenticity, transparency and agency in digital marketing, particularly when young users interact with AI personas they may not recognize as synthetic. Another interesting attempt was made by Riyat et al. (2025). In their paper, “Exploring Youths’ Willingness and Objections to Follow Virtual Influencers Promoting Sustainable Consumption: An Integration of VBN, AIDUA, and SSRIT Frameworks,” they aim to explore the hedonic motivation behind following virtual influencers. The findings highlight that youths’ biosphere values, environmental awareness, sense of responsibility and trust in and emotional connection with virtual influencers play a crucial role in strengthening their willingness to follow and to encourage sustainable lifestyle practices.Attention to the darker side of AI use, particularly in marketing and content delivery, is highlighted by Qadri et al. (2025) and Amin (2025). In Qadri et al.’s (2025) “They Misused Me! Digital Literacy’s Dual Role in AI Marketing Manipulation and Unethical Young Consumer Behavior,” the authors critically examine how a lack of digital literacy among youth in Pakistan may leave them vulnerable to manipulative AI-driven marketing techniques. In addition, the paper “Artificial Intelligence in Social Media: A Catalyst for Impulse Buying Behavior?” by Amin (2025) looks at the region of Brunei and addresses a key research gap by exploring the combined effects of AI-driven recommendations and the visibility of AI-generated labels on impulsive buying behavior. These two publications offer new insights into the role of generational differences and consumer knowledge in shaping responses to AI-based social media marketing. In It underscore the importance of strengthening ethical awareness and digital resilience among young people navigating AI-influenced platforms.As AI technologies evolve rapidly, questions of regulation and institutional accountability become more pressing. In “AI Governance on Young Consumers in Higher Education: A Content Analysis of Policies for Generative AI” by Tong et al. (2025), the authors explore the ethical challenges posed by generative AI and review existing AI policies in higher education aimed at regulating young consumers’ use of such technologies. It focuses on promoting the ethical use of AI, from foundational principles to frameworks for sustainable governance. This contribution situates ethical AI upstream, within institutional settings, underscoring the importance of policy frameworks in protecting and guiding young consumers.A crucial emerging concern relates to the reliability and safety of AI tools used by youth in making purchase decisions. Tan and Leo’s (2025) study, “Safety of LLM-based AI Chatbots for Young Consumers in Purchase Decisions,” investigates the safety of large language model (LLM)-based AI Chatbots for young consumers of Generation Z in their purchase decisions. It highlights that while the use of prompt manipulation techniques on LLMs may be uncommon among these young consumers, such acts are indicative of the young consumer having already developed a precarious attitude or opinion toward a purchase decision, leading to the use of LLMs to guide such decisions.To conclude this special issue, we do not claim to provide definitive answers to the multifaceted relationship between AI and ethical consumerism among young people. Instead, we believe this special issue serves as an essential catalyst for scholars, educators, developers, policymakers and ultimately young consumers themselves to start thinking about the ethical consumption of AI. As guest editors, we are inspired by the diversity of voices and approaches represented in these papers. These contributions collectively highlight the promises and pitfalls as we move toward having a more ethical AI consumerism system.We believe this is just the beginning of a broader conversation and ongoing discovery. Furthermore, it will encourage continued exploration of how AI technologies can be leveraged to reflect, respect and reinforce those moral values. As we move into an increasingly algorithmic society, the ethics of youth consumption will not be a niche concern. It will be a defining question of our collective future.We want to thank all the authors who contributed to this special issue for their insights, creativity and commitment. We also acknowledge the anonymous reviewers and the Young Consumers Editor-in-Chief, the Associate Editor and the editorial team for their support throughout this process.Both AI and young consumers will shape our future. May this special issue contribute to the ongoing conversation to create a better one.

title: Guest editorial: Corporate digital responsibility in hospitality and tourism in the International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is the comprehensive integration of digital technologies into all aspects of organizational operations, leading to fundamental changes in business processes, models and customer engagement strategies (Carroll et al., 2023; Nadkarni and Prügl, 2021; Vial, 2019). It involves not only the adoption of digital data (i.e. digitization) and digital technologies (i.e. digitalization) but also a cultural shift that promotes innovation, agility and continuous improvement (Westerman et al., 2014). The importance of DT lies in its ability to enhance organizational competitiveness and adaptability in a rapidly evolving digital economy (Vial, 2019). It enables firms to streamline operations, improve customer experiences, make data-driven decisions and foster innovation (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Vial, 2019). The key objectives of DT include enhancing customer-centricity through personalized digital experiences, improving operational efficiency via automation, fostering innovation in products and services, increasing organizational agility and leveraging data analytics for strategic decision-making (Carroll et al., 2023; Nadkarni and Prügl, 2021). When successfully implemented, DT can result in increased revenue, stronger customer loyalty, improved employee productivity, the development of new digital offerings and a sustainable competitive advantage in the global marketplace (Vial, 2019).According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) 2022 survey, more than 60% of corporate managers listed corporate environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors as a primary focus for selecting and prioritizing digital capabilities, and more than 80% of companies have a plan to increase their investments in sustainability (Hutchinson et al., 2022). ESG is an emerging practice and is expected to play an essential role in corporate transition management toward corporate sustainability in hospitality and tourism (Back, 2025). While an increasing number of corporations adopt ESG concepts and practices to improve their corporate sustainability performance and achieve the UN’s 17 sustainable development goals (Back, 2024, 2025), corporate leaders and executives find that putting ESG as the top priority in corporate decisions does not guarantee their market success (Pureza and Lee, 2020).ESG-related opportunities and challenges include decarbonization strategies, carbon net-zero strategies, employee health and safety, modern slavery in the corporate value chain and corporate transparency with regulatory compliance (Lee and Vachon, 2016). As the concept of ESG has multiple types of corporate sustainable development, the characteristics of ESG are complex to focus and implement efficiently without losing corporate competitiveness (Lee and Gunarathne, 2021). Achieving ESG goals as a competitive advantage requires integrating digital data, technology, and capabilities into corporate sustainability management. In particular, rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) applications (e.g. service robots, chatbots, generative AI) and DT bring positive impacts and also critical ethical dilemmas to service firms and customers (Dogru et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2023; Wirtz et al., 2023) and selection biases in social media platforms (Zheng et al., 2024). Thus, corporate digital responsibility (CDR) is considered a critical tool and corporate strategy to accelerate service firms’ sustainable transitions and development in the DT era (Lobschat et al., 2021).CDR refers to the principles underpinning a service firm’s ethical, fair, and protective use of data and technology when engaging with customers within their digital service ecosystem (Writz et al., 2023, p. 173). Since diverse AI applications are based on heavy use of corporate and customer data for service innovation (Park et al., 20233), disruptive innovation (Lee et al., 2023) and machine learning (ML) based predictive modeling (Lee et al., 2021), CDR plays a critical role in measuring business performance and creating culture, processes and behaviors for sustainable business success. In hospitality management, CDR is related to various issues, including ethical, social, technological, economic and environmental issues (Lee et al., 2025). Based on these five core elements of CDR in hospitality and tourism, we define CDR as “the set of shared values and norms in the digital ecosystem, requiring proactive governance and voluntary-based guidelines of digital technologies and data management to ensure ethical, social, technological, economic, and environmental aspects and conduct secure, transparent, and sustainable digital practices that foster stakeholders’ trust and well-being” (Lee et al., 2025).Furthermore, AI and ML brought new digital capabilities to various industries (George and Schillebeeckx, 2022). ESG digitization, transferring analog data to digital data, has increased the visibility of CDR practices to various stakeholders in business sustainability and performance in the DT era. Demands for accountability drive companies to disclose their environmental and social footprint for ESG reporting. Connecting digital capabilities to the CDR and ESG agenda enables the management of current ESG-related challenges and opportunities more efficiently and effectively. Therefore, this special issue aims to enhance our understanding of CDR and ESG digitization in corporate sustainability management and digital transformation for hospitality and tourism organizations. In particular, this special issue presents 11 cutting-edge research papers about perceptions toward CDR practices and communication, CDR outcomes, and ESG practices and performance for various stakeholders (i.e. consumers, employees, firms) in the hospitality and tourism context.von Richthofen and Culiberg (2025) develop a conceptual framework for CDR in the sharing economy by extending the value–balance–accountability (VBA) model to include digital irresponsibility and associated tensions. Using Airbnb and Uber as illustrative cases, the authors categorize CDR into three dimensions: value (economic, social and environmental), balance (algorithmic governance, dynamic policy alignment and mediation) and accountability (transparency, trustworthiness, equality and privacy). The authors highlight how SE platforms generate value but also risk value destruction through misrepresentation, discrimination, and privacy violations. The framework presents tensions between stakeholder interests, such as autonomy versus control and transparency versus privacy, and shows how platforms navigate conflicting institutional logics. By integrating CDR into the VBA framework, the study contributes to both sharing economy, CSR, CDR literature, offering a holistic view that captures responsible and irresponsible digital practices. Practical implications include guiding sharing economy platforms, regulators, and policymakers in assessing digital conduct and managing stakeholder tensions. The authors call for future research to explore the framework’s applicability across sectors and deepen the understanding of digital responsibility in platform governance.Kang et al. (2025) demonstrate the interactive effects of corporate privacy responsibility (CPR) and customer education (CE) on consumer responses in the smart hotel context. Using a 2 × 2 experimental design, the study reveals that when hotels demonstrate strong privacy practices and simultaneously educate customers about digital services and practices, consumers show significantly higher levels of trust, more favorable brand attitudes and stronger intentions to visit. The study employs the source–outcome of trust theory and the elaboration likelihood model (ELM) to explain these effects, showing that CE enables central route processing, whereby consumers engage deeply with privacy-related information and form durable trust-based evaluations. In contrast, low CE leads to peripheral processing, relying on superficial cues. The study further finds that trust mediates the relationship between CPR and brand attitudes, which in turn lead to visit intentions. These findings underscore the importance of integrating ethical digital practices with consumer empowerment strategies to foster brand credibility and loyalty. The research findings advocate for hospitality firms to prioritize transparency in data handling and to invest in educational tools that enhance customer understanding and engagement in digitally enhanced service environments.Chaudhary et al. (2025) investigate the impact of CDR on green brand equity (GBE) and propose a research framework in which CDR drives sustainability outcomes through three mediators, including green technology (GT), responsible tourism practices (RTP) and responsible marketing. Employing partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), the study demonstrates that CDR significantly enhances the adoption of GT, the implementation of RTP, and the execution of responsible marketing, leading to GBE. By integrating the resource-based view (RBV) and the technology–organization–environment (TOE) framework, this study conceptualizes CDR as a strategic asset that enables hotels to differentiate themselves in an increasingly eco-conscious marketplace. The research findings reveal that transparent digital practices, ethical marketing, and community-engaged tourism initiatives collectively strengthen brand reputation and customer loyalty. By validating multiple sufficient configurations for achieving high GBE, the study offers a nuanced understanding of how digital ethics and sustainability converge to create competitive advantage. Embedding CDR into core hotel operations and branding strategies is essential for cultivating trust, attracting environmentally aware guests, and positioning hotels as leaders in sustainable hospitality.Sung and Lee (2025) explore how interactive ESG communication – specifically mutuality and openness – shapes consumers’ normative perceptions and brand advocacy behavior in the restaurant industry. Grounded in the theory of normative social behavior (TNSB), the study demonstrates that mutuality in ESG messaging significantly enhances descriptive norms, which in turn positively affect both injunctive norms and brand advocacy on social media. Openness, however, does not significantly affect descriptive norms, suggesting that transparency alone may not be sufficient to shape consumer perceptions of normative behavior. The study also reveals that injunctive norms exert a direct influence on brand advocacy and that online group identity moderates the relationship between descriptive and injunctive norms, but not between descriptive norms and advocacy behavior. These findings highlight the importance of two-way, empathetic communication in shaping consumer engagement with ESG initiatives. The authors argue that mutuality fosters a sense of shared values and social validation, which strengthens normative influence and drives advocacy. The study contributes to the ESG and digital communication literature by integrating TNSB with social identity theory and offering actionable strategies for restaurant marketers to enhance consumer engagement through interactive digital platforms.Lin et al. (2025) explore how hospitality employees emotionally and cognitively respond to data breaches, emphasizing the strategic role of CDR within the broader ESG framework. Through a mixed-methods design comprising qualitative interviews, experimental manipulation, and a large-scale survey, the study identifies threat susceptibility as a key antecedent to psychological contract violation (PCV), which in turn influences two distinct behavioral outcomes: customer-oriented deviance (COD) and unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB). The authors demonstrate that employees who perceive their organizations as vulnerable to digital threats are more likely to experience PCV, leading either to rule-bending actions that favor customers or to ethically questionable behaviors aimed at protecting the organization. These relationships are moderated by customer-based perspective-taking and employee–company identification, respectively. The study extends attribution and social exchange theories to explain how employees assess organizational failures and navigate the tension between loyalty and ethical conduct. By integrating CDR into ESG governance, the authors argue for a proactive approach to digital ethics and cybersecurity, offering actionable insights for hospitality firms seeking to enhance resilience and stakeholder trust in the face of digital crises.Shin and Jang (2025) examine the barriers to implementing CDR in the hospitality and tourism industry, emphasizing the impact of psychological and organizational dynamics on employee compliance. Drawing on social identity theory, this study identifies four key barriers – lack of awareness, economic constraints, technological complexity and lack of organizational focus – that contribute to attitudinal ambivalence among employees and reduce their intentions to comply with CDR initiatives. Using SEM and multigroup analysis, the authors demonstrate that attitudinal ambivalence mediates the relationship between perceived barriers and compliance intentions, while organizational trust partially moderates these effects. Notably, economic constraints emerged as the most significant deterrent to compliance, while the lack of organizational focus does not directly affect compliance intentions but positively influences ambivalence. The research findings offer a better understanding of how employees’ psychological responses to organizational challenges shape their engagement with digital ethics. The study provides practical insights for managers to foster trust, reduce ambivalence, and enhance employee alignment with digital responsibility goals, thereby supporting sustainable DT in the hospitality and tourism industry.Ullah et al. (2025) investigate how digital transformational leadership (DTL), digital organizational culture (DOC), and proactive employee behavior (taking charge, TC) influence organizational resilience (OR) in the hospitality sector, with digital corporate social responsibility (DCSR) as a moderating factor. Grounded in dynamic capabilities theory (DCT), the study uses a time-lagged survey of 380 hotel employees in Beijing, China, and applies structural equation modeling to test direct, mediated, and moderated relationships. Findings reveal that DTL significantly enhances OR, both directly and indirectly through DOC and TC, with a serial mediation effect confirming that DTL fosters a digital culture that empowers proactive behavior, which in turn strengthens resilience. DCSR positively moderates the DTL–OR relationship, suggesting that ethical digital practices amplify the impact of leadership on resilience. The study contributes to DCT by integrating ethical and cultural dimensions into the resilience-building process and highlights the importance of leadership-driven digital agility in collectivist contexts. Managerial implications include fostering a supportive digital culture, incentivizing proactive employee initiatives and embedding ethical digital strategies to enhance adaptability and stakeholder trust in times of disruption.Lunkes et al. (2025) examine how online guest reviews and hotel digital responsibility (HDR) – a hospitality-specific extension of CDR – influence ESG practices and sustainability performance. Using data from 196 Brazilian hotels and over 212,000 TripAdvisor reviews, the study applies sentiment analysis and SEM to assess how positive and negative ESG-related comments affect HDR. The findings reveal that positive social-related reviews enhance HDR, while negative governance-related reviews diminish it. Environmental reviews, whether positive or negative, show no significant impact, likely due to their limited visibility to guests. HDR, in turn, significantly improves environmental, social, and governance practices, which collectively enhance hotel sustainability performance. The study introduces HDR as a strategic framework that bridges digital stakeholder engagement with operational sustainability, emphasizing the role of ethical digital practices in translating guest feedback into actionable ESG strategies. This study offers methodological innovations by combining text mining with ESG measurement and provides practical guidance for hotels to develop automated sentiment monitoring systems and integrate digital feedback into sustainability planning. The research contributes to the evolving discourse on digital ethics in hospitality, highlighting the importance of responsive and transparent digital governance in achieving long-term sustainability goals.Kim et al. (2025a, 2025b) investigate how hospitality firms can enhance ESG performance through the development of digital dynamic capabilities (DDC) and CDR. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and stakeholder theory, the study conceptualizes DDC as comprising digital sensing, seizing and reconfiguring, and examines their influence on both substantive and symbolic CDR. Using survey data from 257 hotel firms across 42 countries and PLS-SEM, the authors find that all three DDC elements positively affect both forms of CDR. Substantive and symbolic CDRs, in turn, significantly improve ESG digitization, which mediates their impact on ESG performance. Notably, neither form of CDR directly enhances ESG performance, underscoring the critical role of digitization as a bridging mechanism. The study also confirms the mediating roles of CDR and ESG digitization in the relationship between DDC and ESG outcomes. These findings advance the literature by differentiating the strategic roles of substantive and symbolic digital responsibility and by positioning ESG digitization as a key operational conduit for sustainability transformation. The authors offer practical guidance for hospitality managers to align digital transformation with ESG goals through responsible digital practices and investment in digital infrastructure.Deng et al. (2025) explore the implementation of environmental technology (ET) in hotels and its impact on green performance, using a dual-theoretical lens of technology affordance and constraint theory (TACT) and the imbrication framework. Through a sequential mixed-methods design – comprising a multiple-case study of 11 hotels and a survey of 364 properties in Hong Kong and mainland China – the study identifies a three-stage ET implementation process: perception, preparation, and actualization. Two key imbrications emerge: green governance, which links perception and preparation, and employee training, which bridges preparation and actualization. The authors find that green governance directly enhances green performance, while employee training and customer engagement serially mediate this relationship. The study introduces a TACT-imbrication framework that captures the dynamic interplay between technological affordances, organizational constraints, and socio-technical adaptation. Quantitative analysis confirms the robustness of the model and highlights the central role of human agency in enabling ET to fulfill its sustainability potential. The research contributes to the hospitality literature by unpacking the micro-level mechanisms of ET implementation and by extending the TOE framework to sustainability contexts. Managerial implications include the need for strategic alignment, cross-functional training and stakeholder engagement to optimize ET deployment and achieve measurable environmental outcomes.Kim et al. title: The Transformative Potential of AI Chatbots in Hearing Health Care
abstract: As Thembi, a 6-year-old female in a remote village, steps into school for the first time, her excitement is overshadowed by an invisible barrier. Struggling to follow lessons and interact with peers, her symptoms of hearing loss remain unnoticed, reflecting a widespread challenge in low- and middle-income countries where access to hearing health care is limited. Imagine her parents’ relief when they connect with a freely available AI health chatbot. Sharing their concerns, they are guided to recognize signs of chronic ear infections—a common yet often overlooked cause of hearing loss in children. The chatbot’s advice leads them to a local primary healthcare clinic, where the detailed feedback helps the nurse identify and treat Thembi’s reoccurring condition. This turning point in Thembi’s life illustrates the transformative potential of AI chatbots in bridging the accessibility gap in hearing health care, offering early detection and intervention that can change the course of a child’s development and quality of life. Thembi’s story is far from unique; millions of children and adults alike, in low-income and high-income countries, face similar barriers, struggling to access the hearing healthcare they desperately need. This situation highlights the reality of access to care for most people affected by hearing loss but also demonstrates the urgent need for innovative solutions that can bring hope and essential services in a timely manner.Figure 1: AI chatbots providing community-based access to hearing care. DALL·E-created artwork; Prompt: De Wet Swanepoel.Table 1: Examples of AI Chatbot Use Case in Hearing Health Care.Thembi’s story, set against the backdrop of the World Health Organization’s 2021 World Report on Hearing,1 illustrates not just the personal impact of hearing health disparities but also the global challenge of unequal access and the critical shortage of health care professionals. The emergence of digital technologies especially access to smartphones in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) heralds a groundbreaking shift. AI chatbots, leveraging this digital surge, could emerge as powerful tools to democratize hearing healthcare.2 By offering an accessible first point of contact, these digital assistants are able to provide immediate, understandable, and actionable health advice, paving the way for a more inclusive health care system. This evolution underscores the potential of technology to transcend barriers, ensuring that geographical distance or socioeconomic status no longer dictates one’s access to essential healthcare services. It sets the stage for a deeper exploration into how AI chatbots could revolutionize hearing health care access, early detection and intervention strategies, making a profound difference for those in dire need. BACKGROUND AND CURRENT CHALLENGES Despite significant advancements in health care, the realm of hearing health faces profound challenges globally. The scale of hearing loss paints a concerning picture: over 1.5 billion people live with some degree of hearing loss, with a projection that this number could soar to over 2.5 billion by 2050.3 Crucially, the vast majority of these cases are found in LMICs, where access to hearing health care professionals is severely limited. In Africa, for example, there are less than 1 audiologist for every million people. This scarcity is compounded by a global inequality in health care access, leaving many without the means to seek or receive treatment. Even in high income countries such as the United States, audiologist are mostly based in metro counties where individuals with higher median income and younger population live creating a hearing health care access issue for older adults who generally have hearing difficulties.4 The impact of hearing loss is multifaceted and far-reaching, affecting individuals’ communication abilities, education, employment opportunities, and overall quality of life. Preventable causes, such as ear infections, account for a significant portion of hearing loss cases, underscoring the urgent need for early detection and intervention strategies. Yet, the gap between those requiring care and the available services is widening, driven by a shortage of skilled professionals and the inaccessibility of existing health care infrastructures in many regions. This backdrop sets a critical stage for exploring innovative solutions, such as AI chatbots, to bridge this gap and offer a beacon of hope for millions. POTENTIAL OF AI CHATBOTS IN HEARING HEALTH CARE The potential of AI chatbots across various sectors, particularly in health care, is met with growing optimism for several compelling reasons.5 Firstly, the technology itself is advancing rapidly, enhancing its capability to understand and interact in increasingly sophisticated and helpful ways. This rapid improvement suggests that AI chatbots could soon provide unprecedented support in diagnosing and managing health conditions, including hearing healthcare. Secondly, the potential for swift and widespread adoption of AI technologies, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), is facilitated by the global proliferation of mobile technology. This widespread mobile penetration offers a solid foundation for deploying AI chatbots to vast populations with minimal infrastructural changes. Lastly, the acute shortage of healthcare professionals in LMICs, a challenge that severely limits access to care, positions AI chatbots as a critical solution to extend health care services to underserved areas. In hearing health care, AI chatbots can emulate successful applications from other health care fields, such as conducting preliminary symptom checks and guiding patients to the appropriate level of care. This approach not only streamlines the use of scarce health care resources but also ensures that individuals with hearing concerns receive timely and accurate advice. Considering the inaccessibility and poor state of health care in LMICs, hearing health care perhaps even more so, even imperfect AI tools may be a dramatic improvement to existing systems.5 Further, the round-the-clock accessibility and anonymity provided by AI chatbots can encourage more people to seek assistance for hearing issues, breaking down barriers to care. By leveraging the general advancements of AI technology and addressing the unique challenges within LMICs, AI chatbots hold the promise of significantly enhancing the accessibility and quality of hearing health care, making them a beacon of hope for millions in need of hearing services. In hearing health care, this translates to AI chatbots not only offering initial hearing screenings and advice on assessments but also educating users on preventative hearing care, identifying potential risks to hearing health, and guiding individuals on when and how to seek further evaluation from healthcare professionals. By drawing parallels with the successful deployment of AI chatbots in other medical fields, we can envision a comprehensive digital health assistant tailored for hearing health. This assistant could support individuals through the entire process of identifying hearing loss, navigating them through self-management tips for minor issues, and streamlining referrals to specialists when necessary. This expanded role exemplifies how AI chatbots could significantly enhance the accessibility and efficiency of hearing health care services, offering a scalable solution to meet the global demand. AI USE CASE EXAMPLES To illustrate the potential of AI chatbots in hearing health care, we can draw from analogous use cases in other medical fields, as well as emerging examples within audiology itself. These examples not only demonstrate the versatility and capability of AI but also shed light on how similar approaches can be adapted to meet the unique challenges of hearing health care (see Table 1). AI Image Analyses. In dermatology, AI-powered applications have revolutionized preliminary assessments by -analyzing images of skin lesions uploaded by users. This innovation offers a preliminary evaluation and recommendations for follow-up care, showcasing AI’s ability to conduct complex visual assessments. The relevance of this to hearing health care lies in its demonstration of AI’s potential for conducting similarly complex assessments, such as evaluating symptoms, understanding communication issues in complex listening situations, analyzing audiograms or classifying otoscopic images.3 Mental Health Chatbots and Long-term Support Mental health chatbots have become instrumental in providing -continuous support and intervention. Their ability to maintain engagement and deliver personalized advice over time exemplifies the chatbot’s potential for long-term patient support.6 Applying this model to hearing healthcare, AI chatbots could similarly monitor a user’s progress in managing hearing loss,7 offering customized advice and reminders for hearing protection or rehabilitation exercises. This example underscores the importance of ongoing, personalized care in managing health conditions, including hearing loss, tinnitus, and hyperacusis, which tend to cause mental health issues such as anxiety and depression. AI Chatbot For Health Care Advice. A recent study in otolaryngology investigated ChatGPT’s ability to accurately respond to patient inquiries.8 By submitting 30 patient questions to ChatGPT (version 3.5), the authors analyzed the AI’s performance from both medical professionals’ and laypersons’ perspectives. The study demonstrated ChatGPT’s impressive accuracy (98.3%) in providing medical information as rated by otolaryngologists. A key finding, however, was that patients may find it difficult to trust information -generated by AI, and this needs to be addressed. Similar work has been done for audiological questions which also demonstrates its potential across different AI large-language models.9 Supporting Primary Health Care. In primary health care environments, AI chatbots have the potential to assist community health workers by offering accurate information and advice on basic ear and hearing care, anchored in clinical guidelines.5 This approach aligns with the World Health Organization’s recent advocacy for task-shifting and innovative technologies in hearing care within LMICs, a strategy recommended due to the pervasive scarcity of hearing health professionals.1 More importantly, AI chatbots can guide patients on when to seek medical attention by evaluating their symptoms and advising on whether their condition requires routine, urgent, or emergency care, along with suggesting appropriate next steps for treatment. Education And Prevention. Pioneering projects are exploring the use of chatbots for educational purposes.5 In hearing care this could enable users to learn about aspects of hearing loss, tinnitus, and hearing conservation and risks associated with occupational and recreational noise exposure. A proactive approach in hearing health can support prevention of hearing loss by providing immediate, accessible advice. The significance of this lies in the chatbot’s ability to offer preventative education and awareness, highlighting an essential component of hearing health that goes beyond treatment to include prevention and awareness. Real-Time Assessments And Feedback. AI can also be instrumental in the deployment of ecological momentary assessments via smartphone applications where AI could provide real-time feedback to patients and clinicians. This approach, for example, could allow for the instantaneous analysis of voice notes through advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Such analyses could be leveraged by specialized AI chatbots designed to deliver immediate, context-specific support tailored to the user’s needs, whether related to their device or environment. This enables a highly personalized assistance experience, providing users with the right support at the precise moment it’s needed. This is especially relevant now, as most hearing aids come with associated smartphone apps, which offer a platform for integrating AI chatbots. These use cases underscore the versatility of AI chatbots in health care, suggesting a promising avenue for their application in hearing health. By leveraging AI’s capabilities for assessment, education, and continuous support, chatbots can significantly contribute to early detection, prevention, and management of hearing loss, making health care more accessible and efficient (Table 1). CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES Implementing AI chatbots in hearing health care presents its set of challenges, such as ensuring accuracy in diverse linguistic and acoustic environments and maintaining patient confidentiality. However, the opportunities for growth are immense, particularly with the increasing penetration of digital technologies in LMICs. This trend not only supports the deployment of AI chatbots but also magnifies their potential impact on health care accessibility. As digital literacy and infrastructure continue to improve, the integration of AI chatbots with mobile phone health apps and telehealth services can expand, enhancing personalized care and facilitating continuous support. Embracing these technological advancements opens a path toward a more inclusive, responsive, and efficient future for hearing healthcare, particularly in underserved settings. Moreover, navigating the ethical landscape, including the development of guidelines for responsible use by consumers, patients, and health care providers, is crucial. Proactively addressing these challenges, while capitalizing on the digital opportunities, charts a promising trajectory for revolutionizing hearing healthcare. Furthermore, to ensure the accuracy and relevance of the responses provided by AI chatbots, it is essential to create and utilize training datasets that are diverse and free of bias, encompassing various languages and cultural contexts. CONCLUSION In conclusion, Thembi’s story and the exploration of AI chatbots in hearing healthcare showcase a future where technology enables new models of care that can transcend traditional barriers, enhancing access and hope for many. The adoption of AI chatbots for early detection, patient education, and ongoing support signals the onset of a transformative era in healthcare. Such progress demands a united front in research, technology development, and policymaking to ensure that advances are ethically sound and universally accessible. Prioritizing accessibility, overcoming language and cultural barriers, and addressing ethical considerations are imperative to ensure quality hearing care is universally available, transcending geographical and socio-economic limitations. By addressing these challenges and harnessing the power of digital innovation, we can evolve hearing health care into a fundamental right, turning success stories like Thembi’s into the norm, rather than the exception.

title: Medication Safety in Australia: Reflecting on the Past, Navigating the Present, and Envisioning the Future
abstract: The names of the patients whose lives we save will never be known. Our contribution will be what did not happen to them. Donald Berwick More than 25 years after To Err Is Human highlighted that an alarming 98 000 hospital inpatients die annually from medical errors and adverse events,1 patient safety continues to challenge healthcare systems, including our own. The burden of patient harm has led to medication safety becoming a global health priority2 and is a formally recognised national standard for Australian hospitals.3 For pharmacists, this is both a validation of our role and a call to action. From handwritten scripts and manual dispensing to integrated digital platforms, dispensing robots, automated dispensing cabinets, and smart pumps, many exciting changes are currently in play and need to be embedded to optimise patient safety. The next exciting journey is the emerging artifical intelligence (AI) tools and the evolution of medication safety into the future must be shaped by pharmacists at every step. Our profession has driven improvements in system accuracy, accountability, and communication, mostly behind the scenes, but always at the heart of safer and more effective patient care. This special issue of the Journal of Pharmacy Practice and Research, the first within a decade, reflects how far we have come and where we are headed. It highlights the innovations that are reshaping medication safety today and asks what the future might look like for pharmacy practice in Australia over the next 20 years. The current landscape of medication safety in Australia is shaped by a confluence of national standards, technological advancements, and our evolving clinical roles. The newly updated Advanced Pharmacy Australia Medication Safety Standards,4 align with the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Patient Safety Challenge, and underscore Australian hospital pharmacists' commitment to system-wide safety and accountability.2 These standards provide a robust framework to guide a reduction in medication harm and foster a culture of continuous improvement to prevent future harm. Recent evidence also highlights the continued growing challenge of polypharmacy across all age groups, with a scoping review featured in this issue, identifying a lack of validated deprescribing frameworks for adults aged under 65,5 underscoring the urgent need for targeted strategies to optimise medication use and safety beyond geriatric care. The future of medication safety depends on empowered pharmacists, smarter systems, and a relentless focus on error prediction and prevention. While this edition does not cover every exciting change in practice, it highlights the core principles driving safer medication use. Imagine it is 2045. As a prescribing pharmacist, you begin your day with all necessary information at your fingertips, courtesy of your AI-enabled robot that has synthesised and organised information overnight from electronic health records, wearable devices, and mobile health apps. You prescribe medications in real-time, with doses tailored to patient symptoms, preferences, and biometrics; guided by predictive algorithms that account for genetics, physiological function, body composition, comorbidities, and emerging evidence-based knowledge. All this automation allows you to spend time with your patients to optimise their medication-related needs. Preliminary patient education is delivered via chatbot, in the patient's preferred language and at an appropriate literacy level. You as the pharmacist can add that extra personal touch and ensure patient-centred care. Throughout admission and upon discharge, informatics pharmacists and advanced clinical assistants adjust each patient's wearable parameters (e.g. blood pressure and glucose targets) to reflect new dosing regimens. 3D-printed combination pills are made to improve adherence, and augmented reality is used to continue education in the patient's home. Follow up appointments are scheduled automatically in the patient's digital diary. This future is within reach. The editorial titled From digitisation to transformation: modernising medication safety for the digital age,6 and the systematic review on machine learning models for personalised dosing of oral anticoagulants,7 highlight AI's potential to transform medicine management with unprecedented precision. However, these papers also underscore the need for robust validation, applying principles of implementation science, and evaluation of areas where evidence is limited, such as the impact on workflows and patient outcomes. Bakker's editorial reminds us that while technology holds enormous promise, it is not without risks.6 Machine learning can enhance workflows and improve safety, but only when developed with rigorous oversight and aligned with clinical workflows. Digital systems must be implemented thoughtfully, with strong governance and continuous evaluation to mitigate new risks introduced by automation.8 To navigate this complexity, medication safety in the digital age must include data literacy, user-centred design, algorithmic accountability, and an embedded culture of digital safety. Governance structures must evolve to incorporate clinical expertise into digital decision-making processes. As Bakker argues, this evolution must be underpinned by investment in pharmacist education,6 equipping future practitioners with the knowledge and skills to lead the digital transformation. Pharmacist expertise in medicine management is increasingly embedded in multidisciplinary teams at transitions of care (ToC) and beyond. In this issue, the emerging roles of pharmacists at ToC are explored. Chandra et al.'s scoping review highlights the growing international evidence supporting the integration of pharmacists into general practice teams (GPPs).9 GPPs play a vital role in identifying medication-related problems, improving prescribing appropriateness, and reducing hospitalisations, particularly through post-discharge interventions and chronic disease management. The reach of medication safety is intimately connected to medication effectiveness—safer systems support best care. In the emerging virtual hospital in the home setting, pharmacists are leading the way with complex outpatient antimicrobial dosing and monitoring clinics. The study by Masoum et al. demonstrates how such service models can offer a safe and effective alternative to intravenous therapy for select infections, which can reduce hospital length of stay and healthcare utilisation.10 Similarly, the virtual cardiac hospital in the home pharmacy service study by Nguyen et al., further supports how pharmacist services can be provided in a virtual setting, providing timely and convenient care and improving patient access.11 Culturally safe care and health equity are pivotal to medication safety. Fostering trust, empowering patients to ask questions, and ensuring that communication about medicines is clear, respectful, and tailored to individual needs are crucial. When Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients feel culturally safe, they are more likely to engage in shared decision-making, disclose concerns, and adhere to treatment plans—all of which are essential for safe and effective medication use.12 Without cultural safety, misunderstandings, mistrust, and disengagement can compromise care and increase the risk of medication harm. Embedding cultural safety into pharmacy practice is not just respectful: it is clinically essential. In this issue, we learn more through the study authored by Welch et al., which showcases a significant step forward in the cultural maturity of hospital pharmacists by demonstrating their willingness to engage in reciprocal, respectful learning with Aboriginal Health Workers (AHWs).13 Through the two-way learning program, pharmacists moved beyond traditional clinical roles to embrace culturally safe communication practices, building trust and rapport with Aboriginal patients. This shift can help with a deeper understanding of the cultural interface, working to address power imbalances in health care.13 Pharmacists are experts in medicine management and must position themselves to prevent major harm at all phases of the medication management cycle (prescribing, dispensing, and administration). Evidence for pharmacist prescribing continues to grow and should be fully embraced and applied where it delivers the greatest impact. Collaborative prescribing, especially during ToC and for medically complex patients, can reduce errors and patient harm. However, to be truly effective, pharmacists must take ownership of their prescribing decisions and remain accountable for ongoing outcome monitoring of the patient. AI and digital expansion will support ongoing care. Importantly, collaborative prescribing between pharmacists, doctors, and nurses also creates valuable opportunities for shared decision-making and broader clinical discussion. Patients are much safer when we collaborate and share. Anderson et al. present one health service's experience with the impact of collaborative prescribing on patient safety, patient flow, and pharmacists' workload.14 Yet, technology alone will not guarantee safety. The human element of compassionate care, ethical decision-making, and interprofessional collaboration will remain central. At the heart of this transformation, there is the need for dedicated resources to prepare the workforce for change and to scope and address medication safety concerns. The implementation of medication safety pharmacist positions in hospitals throughout Australia would provide the necessary expertise and leadership to support safer medication practices and drive continuous improvement. As pharmacists, our role will be to harness innovation while staying grounded in the principles of patient-centred care. As Donald Berwick implies, our success can be measured in the number of patients who travel safely through our health system. This special issue captures a snapshot of a medication safety culture in motion. The studies and commentaries reflect both the complexity of medication safety and the ingenuity of those working to improve it. As we look to the future, let us remain committed to learning from the past, embracing the present, and boldly shaping the next chapter of pharmacy practice in Australia. Thank you to the authors, reviewers, and our editorial team who have contributed to this important collection. As stewards of medication safety, pharmacists have never been more essential—or more empowered—to shape the future of patient care. title: Presidential Address to the 2025 Annual Meeting of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons
abstract: Good morning and welcome to Los Angeles for the 75th Annual Meeting of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons (CNS). In 1951 at the end of World War II, a group of neurosurgeons forged by the adversity of war came together to connect. To share experiences and build a community that was the origin of the CNS. Seventy-five years later, the spirit of connection remains at the heart of who we are today. However, we face different challenges now: administrative burden, barriers to care, cuts to research funding, physician burnout. All demand a renewed connection to our community, our leadership, our peak individual potential, and our pursuit of innovation. This week, we celebrate neurosurgery and the people who make it extraordinary. Today, I reflect on these four enduring themes that define us and the CNS: community, leadership, peak performance, and innovation. First, let us talk about community. Dr Steven Miller was a pediatric emergency room doctor when I was in medical school at Columbia. Sadly, he died later in a tragic plane crash. In his time, he was an early pioneer for an emerging movement: humanism in medicine. Dr Miller said, “we must find ways to permeate each and every aspect of medicine with humanism.” He taught us humanism through the radical, but seemingly simple act of listening. Humanism is asking questions but then to stop and truly listen. Listen for two uninterrupted minutes. It is deceptively simple. A small, marginal yet innovative act of open listening: to build trust, connect, and heal. As neurosurgeons, how deeply are we connecting with our patient community? I was a neurosurgery resident here at Los Angeles General Hospital. Nearly half of this community is non-English speaking preferred. I saw firsthand the importance of meeting patients where they are—language-wise, culturally, emotionally. Doctor–patient connection is a challenge. Studies show that patients remember less than half of the informed consent. Lisa Ling, our Dorothy Nash lecturer, said, “it requires time and energy to get invested in other people's stories, but… you emerge a better and smarter human as a result of taking that time.” This is not simply a communication issue; it is about investing in human connection. Technology such as artificial intelligence (AI) will not replace us—it will help us connect more meaningfully. AI-assisted language translation, transcription, decision support tools, patient education, and counseling. AI will minimize administrative burden such as prior authorization. These tools will free us to connect more humanistically. But community is not just our patients. We are a community that connects through shared learning even and especially through difficult experiences—to uplift us as individuals and elevate our community. This early CNS meeting symposium shows we recognized early on the value of discussing our complications for learning. Today decades later, we are still connecting in the same way through our CNS Complications courses. We learn from each other through listening and sharing experiences from our most challenging cases. The cover of the May 2001 issue of Neurosurgery is a visual representation of the isolation we have all felt after a complication. It looks like what today we call burnout. But the path to improvement is not through isolation. Improvement requires community. As Gandhi said, “Freedom is not worth having if it does not include the freedom to make mistakes.” We must protect that freedom by supporting systems that foster learning. Colleen Fogarty says, “It is the practice of medicine because we must build mechanisms to prompt reflection on our work… seeking and incorporating feedback from others on our team. Effective systems protect time for practice and learning.” Our national organizations, including the CNS, empower us by reinforcing these systems for learning throughout our career. Maya Angelou said, “Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better.” Beverly Walters and CNS Past President Mark Hadley taught us this through their pioneering work in guidelines. We build community through efforts like guidelines: asking the right questions, generating science, interpreting data, and sharing knowledge to elevate our practice standards. Advancements in data science—efforts such as the CNS Data Science scholarship—accelerate these processes. Soon, guidelines will be living documents updated in real time. Our community is connecting broader and faster virtually. CNS NEXUS is a digital library of hundreds of peer-reviewed neurosurgical cases—crowd sourced by our members. The CNS+ app has an AI chatbot that generates knowledge from NEXUS cases, CNS webinars, journal articles, and guidelines. Our Editor-in-Chief, Doug Kondziolka, and Eric Oermann are developing technology that will allow us to interact with the neurosurgical literature in innovative ways. Our advocacy work, celebrating 50 years through the CNS/American Association of Neurological Surgeons Washington Committee, is another expression of community. Thank you to past director Katie Orrico, current director Charlotte Pineda, and CNS Past Presidents Russ Lonser and Alex Khalessi for connecting our specialty to national policy. Community is a connection that breaks barriers to care, elevates our clinical practice, and affects lives. Our community is built on neurosurgeons connecting as leaders to shape our future. As a spine neurosurgeon, I am proud to stand on the shoulders of a leader like Sanford Larson. Larson fought for neurosurgeons to perform complex spinal instrumentation. Dr Larson led by training the first generation of spine neurosurgeons through workshops like this one at the 1980 CNS Annual Meeting. Leaders like Albert Rhoton, the 28th CNS President and my institution's first chair. Dr Rhoton, most known for leading microsurgical anatomy of the brain, also recognized the importance of spine surgery as a distinct community. Dr Rhoton had the vision to call upon the first joint spine section in 1978. Leaders who faced resistance and overcame adversity. Volker Sonntag and others who stood firm when orthopedics challenged our role in pedicle screw instrumentation. And those who led the effort with our industry partners to fight against the pedicle screw litigation of the 1990s—as detailed by Rusty Rodts in his 2010 CNS Presidential Address. Leaders opening doors and leveling the field. Dorothy Nash, our first woman neurosurgeon, is memorialized by the CNS Nash Lectureship. And neurosurgeon Frances Conley who championed women's rights with exceptional courage, dignity and resilience. The American Board of Neurological Surgery, the organization that certified Frances Conley as just the fifth woman neurosurgeon, is now led by Marjorie Wang and Judy Huang. A testament to the progress their leadership made possible. Leadership is shared vision. It is the CNS Pathways program which opens doors for under-represented minorities. Essential for our community, where less than 5% of neurosurgery residents are Black. It is groups such as the American Society of Black Neurosurgeons and the Neurosurgical Pride Alliance. They are building community for neurosurgeons to be welcomed and to be the next generation of leaders. It is also building future leaders. The CNS Leadership Institute celebrates its 10th year. A program that has trained nearly 200 neurosurgeons in skills such as team building, negotiation, project and change management. Starting with those in early career to those at the executive level, many alumni of the institute—myself as one of the first participants—are now division chiefs, department chairs, program directors, and health system executives. Neurosurgeons are being called up to leadership positions that we previously witnessed from the sidelines. Leadership is a connection to building community, mentoring, opening doors for the next generation, and shaping our future. I love the sport of cycling. Exercise, being outdoors, mental well-being. I love watching the Tour de France and seeing pro cyclists at the highest level—with their dedication to the science of peak performance. The relentless optimization of peak individual potential: fitness, recovery, nutrition, the psychology of winning. Cycling, such as neurosurgery, demands the absolute individual best. What might optimizing peak performance look like for neurosurgery? Our Walter Dandy Orator, Dan Buettner, studies the Blue Zones—communities around the world with different genetics, geography and culture. But they share one thing in common: human longevity and well-being. As we will hear from him, peak human potential is not about a single factor. It is about purpose, connection, and balance. Yet modern healthcare works against these values. Today's healthcare is like Frederick Taylor and his industrial engineering approach to organizational management—structure work in the simplest way to maximize efficiency at any cost. In healthcare, this is hyperstandardization without meaningful thought. Electronic health record templates that are essentially billing widgets. RVU targets. Operating room block utilization. These quantify output, but do not capture humanism in neurosurgery. Consolidation of large health systems eliminating job competition. Scope creep by non-neurosurgeons. Commoditizing neurosurgery. “The sum total of hundreds and thousands of tiny betrayals of purpose—de-valuing the neurosurgeon” (Richard Gunderman). Organizational psychology teaches us that these efficiencies do not drive performance and individual potential. Psychologists Hackman and Oldham demonstrated that to drive performance, we must find in our work skill complexity, autonomy, meaningfulness, identity, and feedback. We must connect with neurosurgery on a multifaceted deeper level to enhance our individual potential. Vital to our future is to preserve these very characteristics of neurosurgery that drive and sustain performance. We must balance efficiency with humanity. And ensure our systems empower, rather than constrain neurosurgeons. I am grateful for neurosurgeons like these who serve at executive levels: college of medicine deans, enterprise leaders. They have the appreciation for the value of the neurosurgeon in an enterprise—the true value of the neurosurgeon as presented by Council of State Neurosurgical Societies Chair Luis Tumialan at the 2023 CNS Annual Meeting. Our neurosurgeon leaders can affect health systems at an enterprise level to protect that which drives motivation, professional satisfaction, and peak performance. We cannot accept burnout as our defining narrative. Instead, we should approach the study of human performance with the same rigor we apply to neurosurgical training. Let us understand the physical, cognitive, and psychological factors that enhance individual potential. Like CNS Past President Joseph Maroon, who at age 85 years, is a vice chair of neurosurgery, researcher, ironman triathlete, and author. Joe teaches the equal balance of work, family, health, and personal growth. Enhancing peak performance requires a balance of purpose, well-being, continuous learning, mentorship, and community. These are the cornerstones of longevity. Ultimately, it is these connections, community, leadership, and individual potential that naturally propel us toward innovation. At the University of Florida, innovation has long defined our culture from Dr Robert Cade inventing Gatorade, William Friedman and Frank Bova's advances in LINAC-based radiosurgery, Richard Fessler and the first in human stem cell transplant, and Brian Hoh's National Institutes of Health funded multicenter CAPTIVA trial. This CNS meeting is another showcase for innovation: over 5000 submitted abstracts, over 900 oral abstracts, nearly 1000 unique speakers, 185 industry partners, and 3 incredible finalists for our CNS Innovator of the Year competition; we will decide this year's winner on Wednesday. Like last year's winner Alexandra Golby who developed a low cost, open-source navigation system for low-income countries. This scale speaks to our neurosurgical community connecting to innovation. Today, we are at an inflection point with the rapid development of artificial intelligence. AI will process massive data to predict disease and model outcomes. This will undoubtedly drive the pace of innovation at an incredible cadence. I had a recent conversation with Rich Byrne, Society of Neurological Surgeons President, about the potential of AI. We started by talking about chess. Rich has a master rating. We talked about my son Carter, whose chess team won first place at the 2023 national team competition. Rich says he first became interested in AI from his love for chess. Grandmasters like Bobby Fisher dedicated their lives to memorizing thousands of game scenarios. But chess has an estimated 10123 scenarios. A computer, DeepBlue, in 1996, did what humans could not. DeepBlue mastered chess and then beat grandmaster Gary Kasparov. Kasparov described his match with DeepBlue at the 2021 CNS meeting. Go is a 4000-year-old game from Asia with 10170 possible scenarios. Google's DeepMind learned it in days and then beat South Korean grandmaster Lee Sedol. Games such as chess have distinct rules. AI can do what humans cannot—process every potential scenario to generate a win. There is no need for imagination. But could a computer trained on thousands of open aneurysm clippings imagine endovascular coiling? Could AI ask the relevant questions: Who do we treat? What is a better outcome? To paraphrase Fredrik Pohl, AI undoubtedly can predict the traffic jam, but could AI have predicted the automobile? We should embrace AI for what it can do that we cannot. But AI has limitations. Current AI large language models can generate near pitch perfect language that itself does not understand—not in the way we understand, like true listening. Large language models generate text by predicting the most likely next token based on the prior set of tokens. Best fitting to statistical patterns—not actual understanding. Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus says about the limits of AI, “Neural networks of various kinds can generalize within a distribution of data they are exposed to, but their generalizations tend to break down beyond that distribution.” “You can't think we are close to artificial general intelligence once you realize that as yet we have no general solution to the outlier problem.” Often it is in the outliers that we find our greatest discoveries. It is the outliers where true breakthroughs emerge. Could AI have imagined Picasso from Michelangelo? Or innovators like Spike Lee—who we heard from yesterday—who disrupted and redefined cinema? We must listen to patients for the outliers, the nuance beyond their data. Ask better questions. What else is possible? And from there, imagine better solutions. D. Graham Burnett writes, “There is more to humanism than the accumulation of facts. AI only knows, but it has not lived. No dataset can resolve the central questions that confront every human being. How to live? What to do? How to face death?” Consider brain tumor scientist Elias Sayour. At the University of Florida, he is developing an AI approach to analyze tumor mRNA data to design personalized immunotherapy. But AI cannot ask: How do we face disease? How do we give hope?
